blocks.html:
The strange world of sight

Seeing is believing, it is said. But, asks Richard Gregory, could it be the other way round?

Two of the great British men of the 17th century, the philosopher John Locke and the physicist Isaac Newton, were both aware that objects are not coloured, and that against all appearances light is not coloured either. This is still not generally recognised even now, 400 years later, because it seems so implausible. Yet it tells us something very important - that perceptions are not identical with what we perceive, and may be very different.

The most accurate historical account of perception is that of the 19th-century German scientist Hermann von Helmholtz. However, it was ridiculed at the time. Von Helmholtz thought that perceptions are unconscious inferences we make based on a combination of clues provided by the eyes and other senses, and knowledge of the world. This idea of unconscious inference for perception preceded, by several years, the psychoanalyst Freud's notion of the unconscious, which was also initially treated with derision because it undermined the notion of humans as pre-eminently rational beings who could be held responsible for their actions and awarded blame or praise accordingly.

Crucially, perception of the present depends on rich, though of course not always correct or appropriate, knowledge from the past. We interpret sense data (what we hear, touch, taste, see and smell) from the present according to what we already know. This raises the question: if we see the present through memory, why aren't past and present confused? The pioneering Russian neurologist Alexander Luria described the case of Mr S, who had a remarkable memory. However, he was prone to just such confusions, for example mistaking seeing his clock for remembering it, and so failing to get up in the morning. This suggests that perhaps an important function of perception is to underline the present. Individual perceptions have a vividness that is rare for memories, which might be how we are able to separate them. Try this: look at something for a few seconds, and then shut your eyes and visualise it in memory. You will almost certainly find that the memory is pale by comparison with the perception. Perhaps this is why past and present are not normally confused. Luria's Mr S had exceptionally vivid memories, and rich synaesthesia (experiencing perceptions from another sense as well as the one being stimulated, such as musical notes experienced as colours), which may be why he confused seeing with having seen.

The complexity of processes involved in how we see first impressed itself on me 45 years ago. With my colleague Jean Wallace, I studied the rare case of Sydney Bradford, a man who had been born blind but, through a corneal graft at the age of 52, suddenly found himself able to see. Almost immediately after the operation he was able to 'see' but he could only see those things that he already knew about, having experienced them through touch. It was his touch memories that enabled him to perceive them with his eyes. When Bradford was first taken to the zoo, he proved utterly unable to see an elephant as he had no knowledge to make sense of his perceptions.

The more recent case in California of Mike May, who was also born blind, is similar. Since his operation, his sight has gradually improved as he learns to see, for example, by understanding how shadows represent depth and tell us about the shape of things. Some of the consequences of May's new-found vision were less happy. He had been a champion blind skier, but following the operation, he would have to shut his eyes while skiing to block out what he now found was a terrifying sight.

But acceptance of this intimate connection between memory and perception, even though it was first noticed in the 17th century, has been slow in brain science. Despite the fact that state-of-the-art brain imaging shows that perception animates parts of the brain associated with both present information and memory, most research on memory and perception is still undertaken as if these were separate processes. Seeing used to be thought of as taking place only in the eyes, and in quite specialised brain regions; but now it seems that half the brain is occupied with seeing, requiring a lot of energy. Perhaps this is why we shut our eyes for a rest.

It is not just extreme cases like Mike May, but also much more common errors of seeing — illusions — that can reveal the crucial role of memory in governing what we (think we) see. Perception depends on specific knowledge and probabilities. Our brains calculate the likelihood of what is out there, and when too far-fetched, perceptions are rejected.

A dramatic and discomforting example is looking at the two sides of a face-mask. From the front it is a convex shape with the nose sticking out. Then if the mask is rotated, the back of the mask will be seen as convex, though we know that it must be concave. It is almost, if not quite, impossible to sketch the back of a hollow mask to look as it is — hollow. Science often learns from what does not happen: people not seeing a hollow face as hollow is the most revealing experiment on perception. The unsettling truth from brain science is that even people with no visual impairment see what, at some level, they expect to see, and often miss things as they really are.

Questions 27–30

Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

27 Why does the writer refer to Locke and Newton in the first paragraph?

28 According to the writer, why was Freud's theory of the unconscious mocked?

29 The writer describes Mr S failing to get up in order to demonstrate

30 What point is the writer making in the text as a whole?

Questions 31–36

Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

  • YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer
  • NO if the statement contradicts the views of the writer
  • NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

31 Sydney Bradford relied on recollections of objects he had been told about to help him see after his operation.

32 People who only start to see as adults can learn to see as other people do in time.

33 People who have gained their sight as adults find certain activities harder to do than before.

34 It is evident now that sight involves the eyes and one particular area of the brain.

35 The mask experiment is particularly useful in training people who are regaining their sight.

36 People with perfect vision can fail to interpret objects correctly under certain circumstances.

Questions 37–40

Complete the summary using the list of words, A–J, below.

The mask experiment

In this experiment, having looked at the front of a simple face-mask, subjects look at the reverse. However, the subjects are convinced that they are still looking at a mask which is 37 in shape. They believe that the 38 is poking out in the normal manner because that is what they are used to seeing. Attempting to make a 39 of the mask in this orientation leads to the same problem. The subjects fail to see a concave form because of the 40 they have that the features of a face stick out.

A back
B brain
C view
D round
E sight
F nose
G convex
H hollow
I drawing
J preconception

meta.title: The strange world of sight 奇异的视觉世界

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 1
passageNotes.text: 17世纪两位伟大的英国人——哲学家John Locke和物理学家Isaac Newton——都意识到物体是没有颜色的，而且与所有表象相反，光也是没有颜色的。即使在400年后的今天，这一点仍然没有被普遍认识，因为它似乎难以置信。然而，它告诉我们一个非常重要的道理——感知并不等同于我们所感知的东西，而且可能截然不同。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 2
passageNotes.text: 关于感知的最准确的历史记述来自19世纪德国科学家Hermann von Helmholtz。然而，这一理论在当时遭到了嘲笑。Von Helmholtz认为，感知是我们在眼睛和其他感官提供的线索组合以及世界知识的基础上做出的无意识推断。这种关于感知的无意识推断思想比精神分析学家Freud的无意识概念早了几年，后者最初也遭到嘲笑，因为它削弱了人类是卓越的理性存在、能够为自己的行为负责并因此受到责备或赞扬的观念。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 3
passageNotes.text: 关键在于，对当下的感知依赖于丰富的（当然并非总是正确或恰当的）过去知识。我们根据已有的知识来解读来自当下的感官数据（我们听到、触摸、品尝、看到和闻到的东西）。这就提出了一个问题：如果我们通过记忆来看当下，为什么过去和现在不会混淆呢？先驱性的俄罗斯神经学家Alexander Luria描述了S先生的案例，他拥有非凡的记忆力。然而，他恰恰容易产生这种混淆，例如将看到时钟误认为是记得它，从而未能在早晨起床。这表明感知的一个重要功能也许是强调当下。个体感知具有一种记忆中罕见的生动性，这可能是我们能够区分它们的方式。试试这个：看某样东西几秒钟，然后闭上眼睛在记忆中想象它。你几乎肯定会发现，与感知相比，记忆是苍白的。也许这就是为什么过去和现在通常不会混淆。Luria的S先生拥有异常生动的记忆和丰富的联觉（在受到一种感官刺激的同时体验到另一种感官的感知，例如将音符体验为颜色），这可能就是他混淆"看到"和"看过"的原因。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 4
passageNotes.text: 45年前，视觉过程中所涉及的复杂性第一次给我留下了深刻印象。我和同事Jean Wallace研究了Sydney Bradford的罕见案例，他天生失明，但在52岁时通过角膜移植突然发现自己能够看见。手术后几乎立即他就能够"看见"，但他只能看到那些他已经通过触摸体验过的东西。正是他的触觉记忆使他能够用眼睛感知它们。当Bradford第一次被带到动物园时，他完全无法看到一头大象，因为他没有知识来理解他的感知。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 5
passageNotes.text: 加利福尼亚州更近期的Mike May案例也是类似的，他同样天生失明。自从手术以来，他的视力随着他学会看东西而逐渐改善，例如，通过理解阴影如何代表深度并告诉我们事物的形状。May新获得的视力带来的一些后果不那么令人愉快。他曾是盲人滑雪冠军，但在手术后，他不得不在滑雪时闭上眼睛，以挡住他现在觉得可怕的景象。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 6
passageNotes.text: 尽管记忆与感知之间的密切联系早在17世纪就被注意到，但在脑科学中接受这一观点的过程一直很缓慢。尽管最先进的脑部成像显示感知会激活与当前信息和记忆相关的大脑部分，但大多数关于记忆和感知的研究仍然是在假设它们是分开的过程的情况下进行的。过去人们认为视觉只发生在眼睛和相当专业的大脑区域中；但现在看来，大脑的一半都在忙于视觉，需要大量能量。也许这就是为什么我们闭上眼睛休息。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 7
passageNotes.text: 不仅仅是像Mike May这样的极端案例，还有更常见的视觉错误——错觉——也能揭示记忆在控制我们（认为自己）看到的东西方面的关键作用。感知依赖于特定的知识和概率。我们的大脑计算外面事物的可能性，当过于牵强时，感知就会被拒绝。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 8
passageNotes.text: 一个戏剧性且令人不安的例子是看面具的两面。从正面看，它是一个凸出的形状，鼻子突出。然后如果面具被旋转，面具的背面也会被看成是凸出的，尽管我们知道它一定是凹陷的。要画出空心面具背面的样子——空心的——几乎是不可能的，即使不是完全不可能。科学常常从没有发生的事情中学到东西：人们看不到空心脸是空心的，这是关于感知的最具启发性的实验。脑科学带来的令人不安的真相是，即使没有视觉障碍的人，在某种程度上也会看到他们期望看到的东西，并且常常错过事物的真实面貌。

items.text:
（1）题目 27：Why does the writer refer to Locke and Newton in the first paragraph?
题目翻译：作者为什么在第一段提到洛克和牛顿？
答案：D（to point out that his notions are not new）
定位：正文第1段，第1至2句
原文：were both aware that objects are not coloured, and that against all appearances light is not coloured either. This is still not generally recognised even now, 400 years later
译文：两人都知道物体并没有颜色，光也没有颜色；即使四百年后的今天，这一点仍未被普遍认识。

解析：作者先列举17世纪的洛克和牛顿已知道这一观点，再说四百年后仍未普遍接受，作用是说明自己的观点早已有之，并非新说。

（2）题目 28：According to the writer, why was Freud’s theory of the unconscious mocked?
题目翻译：作者认为，弗洛伊德的无意识理论为什么受到嘲笑？
答案：C（People felt that it devalued the accepted concept of humanity.）
定位：正文第2段，末句
原文：was also initially treated with derision because it undermined the notion of humans as pre-eminently rational beings
译文：该理论起初也受到嘲笑，因为它削弱了“人类首先是理性存在”的观念。

解析：undermined the notion 对应 devalued the accepted concept；人们觉得理论动摇了既有的人性观，因此选该项。

（3）题目 29：The writer describes Mr S failing to get up in order to demonstrate
题目翻译：作者描述 S 先生没能起床，是为了说明什么？
答案：C（how unusual it is to mistake a perception for a memory.）
定位：正文第3段，中部
原文：mistaking seeing his clock for remembering it, and so failing to get up in the morning
译文：他把看见时钟误以为只是记起时钟，因此早晨没能起床。

解析：案例把“当下知觉”错当成“记忆”，后文说明普通人的知觉通常比记忆鲜明，能够把二者区分开；因此该混淆属于少见情况。

（4）题目 30：What point is the writer making in the text as a whole?
题目翻译：作者在全文中要表达的中心观点是什么？
答案：A（Perception involves much more than the data collected by the eyes.）
定位：正文第2段，第3句
原文：perceptions are unconscious inferences we make based on a combination of clues provided by the eyes and other senses, and knowledge of the world
译文：知觉是我们基于眼睛和其他感官提供的线索以及对世界的知识所作出的无意识推断。

解析：全文反复说明知觉不仅来自眼睛输入，还依赖其他感官、既有知识、记忆和大脑预测，成年复明和面具实验都是对此的例证。

items.text:
（1）题目 31：Sydney Bradford relied on recollections of objects he had been told about to help him see after his operation.
题目翻译：悉尼·布拉德福德术后依靠别人向他讲述物体所形成的记忆来帮助看见。
答案：NO
定位：正文第4段，中部
原文：It was his touch memories that enabled him to perceive them with his eyes.
译文：是他的触觉记忆让他能够用眼睛感知这些物体。

解析：题干说记忆来自别人讲述，原文明确说来自亲手触摸形成的记忆，两者直接矛盾，因此选 NO。

（2）题目 32：People who only start to see as adults can learn to see as other people do in time.
题目翻译：成年后才开始看见的人，最终能够学会像其他人一样看东西。
答案：NOT GIVEN
定位：正文第5段，第2句
原文：Since his operation, his sight has gradually improved as he learns to see
译文：手术后，随着他学习如何看，他的视觉逐渐改善。

解析：原文只说 Mike May 的视觉逐渐改善，没有说明他最终能否达到与普通人相同的水平，也没有给出时间结论，因此选 NOT GIVEN。

（3）题目 33：People who have gained their sight as adults find certain activities harder to do than before.
题目翻译：成年后恢复视力的人会发现某些活动比以前更难。
答案：YES
定位：正文第5段，末句
原文：He had been a champion blind skier, but following the operation, he would have to shut his eyes while skiing to block out what he now found was a terrifying sight.
译文：他曾是盲人滑雪冠军，但手术后滑雪时不得不闭上眼睛，隔绝如今令他恐惧的景象。

解析：Mike May 术前擅长滑雪，恢复视力后视觉反而干扰这项活动，说明某些活动变得更困难，因此选 YES。

（4）题目 34：It is evident now that sight involves the eyes and one particular area of the brain.
题目翻译：现在已经明确，视觉涉及眼睛和大脑中的某一个特定区域。
答案：NO
定位：正文第6段，倒数第2句
原文：Seeing used to be thought of as taking place only in the eyes, and in quite specialised brain regions; but now it seems that half the brain is occupied with seeing
译文：过去人们认为视觉只发生在眼睛和少数专门脑区，但现在看来，半个大脑都参与视觉。

解析：题干把视觉限制在一个特定脑区，原文却说现在看来半个大脑都参与，意思相反，因此选 NO。

（5）题目 35：The mask experiment is particularly useful in training people who are regaining their sight.
题目翻译：面具实验特别适合用于训练正在恢复视力的人。
答案：NOT GIVEN
定位：正文第8段，倒数第2句
原文：people not seeing a hollow face as hollow is the most revealing experiment on perception
译文：人们不能把空心面孔看成空心，是最能揭示知觉机制的实验。

解析：原文只说该实验能够揭示知觉如何运作，没有谈它是否用于训练复明者，因此选 NOT GIVEN。

（6）题目 36：People with perfect vision can fail to interpret objects correctly under certain circumstances.
题目翻译：视力完好的人在某些情况下也可能无法正确理解物体。
答案：YES
定位：正文第8段，末句
原文：even people with no visual impairment see what, at some level, they expect to see, and often miss things as they really are
译文：即使没有视觉障碍的人，也会在某种程度上看到自己预期的东西，并常常错过事物的真实面貌。

解析：no visual impairment 对应视力完好；expect to see 和 miss things as they really are 说明在特定情境下仍会误判，因此选 YES。

原文：He had been a champion blind skier, but following the operation, he would have to shut his eyes while skiing to block out what he now found was a terrifying sight.
译文：他曾是盲人滑雪冠军，但手术后滑雪时不得不闭上眼睛，隔绝如今令他恐惧的景象。

解析：Mike May 术前擅长滑雪，恢复视力后视觉反而干扰这项活动，说明某些活动变得更困难，因此选 YES。

（4）题目 34：It is evident now that sight involves the eyes and one particular area of the brain.
题目翻译：现在已经明确，视觉涉及眼睛和大脑中的某一个特定区域。
答案：NO
定位：正文第6段，倒数第2句
原文：Seeing used to be thought of as taking place only in the eyes, and in quite specialised brain regions; but now it seems that half the brain is occupied with seeing
译文：过去人们认为视觉只发生在眼睛和少数专门脑区，但现在看来，半个大脑都参与视觉。

解析：题干把视觉限制在一个特定脑区，原文却说现在看来半个大脑都参与，意思相反，因此选 NO。

（5）题目 35：The mask experiment is particularly useful in training people who are regaining their sight.
题目翻译：面具实验特别适合用于训练正在恢复视力的人。
答案：NOT GIVEN
定位：正文第8段，倒数第2句
原文：people not seeing a hollow face as hollow is the most revealing experiment on perception
译文：人们不能把空心面孔看成空心，是最能揭示知觉机制的实验。

解析：原文只说该实验能够揭示知觉如何运作，没有谈它是否用于训练复明者，因此选 NOT GIVEN。

（6）题目 36：People with perfect vision can fail to interpret objects correctly under certain circumstances.
题目翻译：视力完好的人在某些情况下也可能无法正确理解物体。
答案：YES
定位：正文第8段，末句
原文：even people with no visual impairment see what, at some level, they expect to see, and often miss things as they really are
译文：即使没有视觉障碍的人，也会在某种程度上看到自己预期的东西，并常常错过事物的真实面貌。

解析：no visual impairment 对应视力完好；expect to see 和 miss things as they really are 说明在特定情境下仍会误判，因此选 YES。

items.text:
（1）题目 37：In this experiment, having looked at the front of a simple face-mask, subjects look at the reverse. However, the subjects are convinced that they are still looking at a mask which is ________ in shape. They believe that the ________ is poking out in the normal manner because that is what they are used to seeing. Attempting to make a ________ of the mask in this orientation leads to the same problem. The subjects fail to see a concave form because of the ________ they have that the features of a face stick out.
题目翻译：受试者确信自己仍看到一个形状为________的面具。
答案：G（convex）
定位：正文第8段，第3句
原文：the back of the mask will be seen as convex, though we know that it must be concave
译文：面具背面会被看成凸起的，尽管我们知道它必定是凹的。

解析：题干问受试者实际感知到的形状，原文明确说背面被看成 convex，因此选择 convex。

（2）题目 38：In this experiment, having looked at the front of a simple face-mask, subjects look at the reverse. However, the subjects are convinced that they are still looking at a mask which is ________ in shape. They believe that the ________ is poking out in the normal manner because that is what they are used to seeing. Attempting to make a ________ of the mask in this orientation leads to the same problem. The subjects fail to see a concave form because of the ________ they have that the features of a face stick out.
题目翻译：他们认为________仍以正常方式向外突出。
答案：F（nose）
定位：正文第8段，第2句
原文：From the front it is a convex shape with the nose sticking out.
译文：从正面看，面具是凸形的，鼻子向外突出。

解析：在脸部特征中，原文直接说向外突出的部位是 nose，因此选择 nose。

（3）题目 39：In this experiment, having looked at the front of a simple face-mask, subjects look at the reverse. However, the subjects are convinced that they are still looking at a mask which is ________ in shape. They believe that the ________ is poking out in the normal manner because that is what they are used to seeing. Attempting to make a ________ of the mask in this orientation leads to the same problem. The subjects fail to see a concave form because of the ________ they have that the features of a face stick out.
题目翻译：尝试从这一方向制作面具的________也会遇到同样问题。
答案：I（drawing）
定位：正文第8段，第4句
原文：It is almost, if not quite, impossible to sketch the back of a hollow mask to look as it is — hollow.
译文：几乎不可能把空心面具的背面画成它真实的空心样子。

解析：sketch 是“画、素描”，题干 make a ___ 需要名词，选项 drawing 与之同义且语法完整。

（4）题目 40：In this experiment, having looked at the front of a simple face-mask, subjects look at the reverse. However, the subjects are convinced that they are still looking at a mask which is ________ in shape. They believe that the ________ is poking out in the normal manner because that is what they are used to seeing. Attempting to make a ________ of the mask in this orientation leads to the same problem. The subjects fail to see a concave form because of the ________ they have that the features of a face stick out.
题目翻译：受试者无法看到凹形，是因为他们有一种脸部特征应向外突出的________。
答案：J（preconception）
定位：正文第8段，末句
原文：see what, at some level, they expect to see
译文：在某种程度上看到他们预期会看到的东西。

解析：expectation 表示事先形成的预期，题干结构 because of the ___ they have 需要名词，preconception 表示先入之见或预设，最符合语义。
